paragraphs: Talented biz-dev people are rare, but that's not the point. The point is that the claim “it's wrong to ask an LLM for X” or “wrong to expect Y from an LLM,” and that instead you should “write … code that correctly pulls the data format out of the right APIs and puts it where it belongs in the right shape” — that claim is exactly where the gap between engineers and everyone else has always grown from.

Except I never expect engineers to do my job even 1% as effectively, while they usually talk as if you're not a human being unless you can … knock out a little script that automates something =) They forget how many tens of thousands of hours went into their specialization, and that it started back in grade school, honestly (that's what the straight A's were for, and the math olympiads).
That is the whole global point of LLMs showing up. Automating anything by hand, with coders, was always possible — for money.

It's just that the money is paid by people who sometimes can't even articulate what they need (a gigantic inefficiency grows), and the same people usually can't check the result either (the gigantic inefficiency gets multiplied by a sack of …). So the world arrived at a place where, if you have no money, you can't afford to … run a business at all, because building something big, sweaty and permanent with coders' hands takes real billions. Something small and … but working — still millions. And where do you get those in a world where, by official numbers, over 25 YEARS a person in the UK on £80k (three times the average salary) saves somewhere between £900k and £1.4m?
OVER 25 YEARS
Which means that “on their own dime” a person can't afford anything development-related in the current economy, and going forward will be able to afford it with ever-decreasing probability.
And then the LLM arrives, which is supposed to make it so that any regular Joe can make his dream come true for a very specific, understandable amount of money.
An LLM is a kind of global standardization of everything. Putting in order, all at once, all the knowledge humanity has accumulated and the practical ways of using that knowledge.

Technically, as long as the question in this chat is “how do I enrich a spreadsheet with just a request” and the answer is “for now, you can't” = the LLM is a concept car that doesn't even have a proper engine in it yet, pre-pre-pre-alpha.

But you can see the bricks — the operators, contexts jumping into the millions, the fabulous growth in accuracy, and so on. It's all slowly converging from every side toward a single point where any regular Joe in this chat tells the LLM “I want this” and “gets the result.” The result may be better or worse, you can argue about prompting and so on. But for now you can't get the result at all without code.)

Guys, among the hundreds of rejections in Novosibirsk before Alawar hired me by accident, I was rejected by a company called Movavi. The HR person said my eyes didn't light up at all and that overall I didn't look neat enough to work at their company.

Three years later, on behalf of Yandex, I closed a deal with Movavi's commercial director and brought them millions of dollars (through distribution of the Yandex Bar). And in 2018 Gleb introduced me to the owners of Movavi, and they consulted me about selling their company outright :D
The only fair hiring happens at the level of the shareholders/founders of a business, regardless of its size.

If you're interviewing or being tested by someone who is NOT the owner of the business (which is the case in the overwhelming majority of situations), don't try too hard to rationalize a rejection, and definitely don't agonize over it.
It's the most talentless way to spend energy. About as useful as whimpering and wringing your hands over why this madman is trying to eat a spoon or reading a book upside down.
It.Just.Happens.And.There.Is.Nothing.You.Can.Do.About.It
But you can move on and find sane people who fit you. They are almost never the first ones, and often not even the fiftieth.

In sales, for example, it would be impossible to work if you took rejections at all dramatically (and those who do take them dramatically don't grow in sales and wither, guaranteed), because you send thousands of emails, get on dozens and hundreds of calls, and receive not just rejection but hundreds of rude remarks of every kind.
The only right way to look for a job: send out no fewer than X a day, go and talk to everyone. Takes a week. Takes six months.
In the end you find what you need, and that's it.
Fucking easy
And the résumé-padders who sell a “guaranteed placement” and shorten the natural path described above with packaged deception — they are the reason you suffer ten times more than you would have to.
By the way, even at the founder/shareholder level, fair hiring happens more often, but far from always.
Just one of hundreds of examples from my memory:

The founder of iSpring was looking for a head of sales; for laughable money I found him 5 people with … careers, incredibly smart, very unique people. He didn't get on a call with any of them, because

“Anton, I looked at the photos of these people. First of all, one of them is a woman. A woman should be making soup, are you joking, offering her to me for sales, and as a manager at that? I thought better of you. As for the other four guys… I see no point in calling them, because I don't see a masculine principle in their faces in the photos. Look at me. In this manly face you can see a man who, if he has to, can bring in the hay on a tractor. Chop firewood. And if a cartridge jams on a hunt, take down a deer with his bare hands. I need people no less, and even more, masculine than me.”

Fortunately I never saw that man again. Also curious: the best results in their company, in units and in dollars, belonged to three young women… That's what happens when you're out riding a tractor instead of watching the CRM.

She couldn't handle the internal pressure — the founder's role is very much about keeping cool. All these urges to predict the outcome translate easily into plain English as “I'm too afraid of screwing up.”
I have quite a few acquaintances aged 35–40 whose last long-term relationship was about 10 years ago, and whose longest ever lasted 2.5 years max.

Obviously there are many gradations of reasons there, but one of the most popular: a failed relationship promises pain during, at the end, and even for some time after it's over. Many people who have been through that pain fall into a kind of loop in their heads: until a relationship shows up like the one in that movie, or even that cartoon, and I get practically assaulted with this golden relationship that I will do everything to hide from — I'm not entering a new one.
Sometimes the chemistry kicks in and they open up to someone and enter a relationship, but then in the process they get … scared and do everything to end it as fast as possible.
The mechanics with founders are similar.
And the market is full of course-sellers and consultants of every kind who tell people not what works but what they want to hear.

So people get told that the way they're doing it is the way it should be done. All correct. Whatever you do — all correct. That'll be $250, by the way. Remember — you're doing everything right. If you keep doing everything right, next week that'll be another $250.

So for decades a person runs around looking for metrics that don't exist, writing business plans around them. Skimping on people, because “alone it … won't work out with anyone anyway, so why overpay,” and so on.
It amuses me that year after year middle managers tell me what SalesBomb's clients would find interesting.
Reminder: I closed 650 deals with SalesBomb clients who paid me upfront, in various years, from 8 to 25 thousand dollars a month without any guarantees, and many of them worked with me for years.
I very much doubt there is another Russian speaker who has closed as many deals, in dollars, selling outsourced biz-dev/lead-gen on terms as vague as ours =)))
I doubt anyone has closed even half as many.
But of course guys will keep dropping in to advise me on what SalesBomb's clients would like =)

Honestly, I … the potential SalesBomb clients who would want me to expose other people's businesses on a drunken …. Those aren't clients, they're bums. Real clients sign NDAs with us so strict that I'm not always sure we're allowed to do our own core business, since you'd have to tell someone something by email, and the lawyers try to choke us so we can't even say the company's name out loud)))

By the way, the market is already somewhat … wary of me (that concern has been read to me many times and I've lost heaps of clients because of it) thanks to my, let's say, unorthodox YouTube activity and sharp tongue on Facebook, where every now and then I mention someone and dissect the chronicle of his … in detail. Have you heard anything like that, in that volume, from anyone who isn't in the course-selling business? =)
Sure, let me … nail myself to a cross too, to prove something to someone.
As if I have nothing … better to do :))))))

And if you're too lazy to go back through my old content and dig all this up — well then … off, and that's that. You're even allowed to talk badly about me, it's not forbidden. As the classic said: “when I'm not there, they're even allowed to beat me!”

No, Sanya isn't crowned in that sense at all; on the contrary, he explained to me that my audience is of incredible quality, and that on YouTube, as on Facebook, in a Telegram channel or anywhere else, what matters isn't the numbers but the people behind them, their cohorts and extremes, their concentration, and so on.
It's obvious to a horse that you can get more value out of 100 people who own venture funds than out of 5 million viewers of a channel that shows how to bake cabbage pies properly.

If, of course, the goal isn't likes and $5k sponsored integrations, but business projects or the by-products of high-level networking, or whatever else you can get from the attention of a crowd of investors.

Everyone's goals are different. Right now in the group for big YouTubers I see people very actively discussing how to monetize an audience, that you need to spin up side businesses because ad revenue is … dropping.
Many guys are shutting down channels that have 3 million views on their latest videos.
People who don't have channels of their own don't realize that you can have 500k subscribers and millions of views on your videos and still be sitting there … with no butter, sucking on pennies.
Meanwhile you can have 1,000 subscribers and, if they're interested in your business with big checks and margin, make millions of dollars off that grand.
Monetization in social media in general correlates very weakly with the obvious numbers.
Bro, forget what the guys on the Internet say. A thought, once spoken, is a lie =)
The real players don't say anything to anyone anywhere on this topic — that's the solution to this thrilling riddle.)
I know a guy who single-handedly built an entire EMPIRE on plugins for Jira and Salesforce/HubSpot.
He simply … out 2 plugins a week.
Out of every 50 plugins, one took off to the point of bringing in about $1k a month.
And one plugin took off so hard it started bringing in $10k a month.
Sounds like …, but over 5 years he got to the point where his plugins, with the long tail, brought in enough that he sold his business for $7 million.)
And before that, all that time, he was earning, let's say, not badly either — he was definitely clearing 50–70k a month.
Unfortunately he doesn't talk about it on YouTube =)
In B2B, to sell it's simply not enough to LISTEN TO OTHER PEOPLE'S TALES ABOUT PROBLEMS.
Until you've held a candle over the problems for many, many thousands of hours, you still won't understand them.
The trick isn't the problem itself, but what makes it a problem.
Very many B2B products, not understanding this important detail, rush to build something and flop.
Because the reason certain buttons don't get clicked turns out to be nothing like what they thought)) They thought people lacked the right buttons.
Turns out people are just losers ….
And that, alas, you can't vibe-code away.
Bingo. Most solutions that in the laboratory appear to perform a very useful function very well end up never being used by anyone except the lab assistants of that laboratory.

For anyone to use your … you need to know not the problem, but everything inside the organization that frames the problem, gives birth to it, the economics of that problem across the most varied departments, and so on and so forth.
Take my genuinely successful acquaintances who live very well in B2B — they can explain their clients' business TO THE CLIENTS far better than THE CLIENTS understand it themselves =)
If you can't explain and sketch a logistics company's entire business on a napkin for them, there's no point trying to build them technical solutions.
A simple example:

We had a client who claimed his research showed that every construction company in America needed to reduce the rate of foot diseases (already funny) among workers on site, so he raised $500k for an app that scans your foot (actually just a GIF, … there wasn't even any technology) and shows how badly a worker's foot is developing, letting you preventively head off his foot … and back pain.
I'm thinking, well, … knows, but the guy says they did a study, everyone desperately needs it ….
We went to sell — nobody answers.
I went to acquaintances who are the second-largest construction company in California.
The owner of that construction company is straight-up my buddy.
He listened to me for literally 40 seconds.
And he goes, … Tim, come on, … you too, for crying out loud
You know, he says, what health problems my workers have?
They … don't put on HARD HATS on super dangerous sites
And they get their HEADS … CRACKED OPEN
Healthy feet aren't going to help there, he says, you understand?
The guy, like, lived and lived and died …
Right on my CONSTRUCTION SITE
And you know what else, he says?
They don't clip in!
The dumb ape, he says, climbs up the boom to a height where birds freeze
And he says the … idiot forgot to clip in, and of course he … right at the moment he forgot — that's how it works
You, he says, fix THAT … for me
And then, after another 15 problems that also need solving, more serious ones, maybe we'll get around to the nice healthy feet of these …
But actually, he says, I'll tell you a little secret — we won't get there. I … the ones with sore feet, you know what I do with them? I FIRE them

… he says, construction workers with sore feet? For every worker with healthy feet I've got 500 Mexicans standing in line who'd win an Olympic medal in running tomorrow if that's what it took to get the job
So, he says, take those startup fairy tales and shove them up the … of whoever told them to you
And go do something useful =)
Dunno, the only thing I can suppose is one of two things:
1) I didn't sit there for 5 hours, but 100+, before anything seriously moved off the dead center for me.
2) Because of your professional deformation you can close your eyes to the limitations, while I, on the contrary, look for them in order to use them, since they are the only channel I have.
For example: you know exactly how the cropper task should be done, and the LLM can't do it that (correct) way.
So you get indignant and think the LLM is dumb.

Whereas someone like me, who has no idea how such a task should be done, will end up poking at it this way and that, and will notice that cropping the photo along one line works pretty reliably, and the problem is with the remaining three lines.
So I'll just … together a kludgy script that cuts four times along one line, and enjoy a working cropper, while you sit and wait for it to start coding for you the way you know how.)
Maybe a bad example, but I know it's true to life, because I see it in my buddies — deep coders who don't use LLM coding because looking at clumsy-ish code drives them nuts.)

And the fact that this code is free, unlike beautiful code — unfortunately only entrepreneurs understand the value of that phrase, and not all of them, mostly those who can't code themselves or haven't wanted to for too long, or older people who have long been … with everything in principle, and to whom any automation is by default perceived as ….)
There's an opinion that vibe-coding and coding are fundamentally different things. And one gets in the way of the other very, very badly =)

Also, vibe-coding needs ferocious stamina, because unlike a coder's stamina, where a person knows in principle what has to be done and it's just tedious, in vibe-coding the person doesn't know what has to be done and doesn't even know whether it will work, or whether it's even possible. So you really have to sit there and bang your head against the wall =)

For example, I don't even expect many of my acquaintances to vibe-code anything until some AGI shows up that does everything for them from a single prompt, because they don't have enthusiasm for more than 40 minutes even on clear tasks. Accordingly, the only processes that work for them are ones whose result fits in a 40-minute window. Hanging other processes on them is pointless — it'll just be a death loop.
If I have 40 minutes for vibe-coding, I won't even open Cursor. The minimum useful outcome in a day takes 3–5 hours to reach; whether it's 3 or 5 depends on luck :D
Also funny that when I was working on the bot, many people asked, like, … are you spending your precious time so inefficiently? You've sunk more into this bot than it would cost to pay a coder…
Many people greatly overestimate the usefulness of an entrepreneur's average working hour =)

Entrepreneurship is essentially the same vibe-coding, only across all of surrounding reality. Sometimes to earn $10k of NEW BUSINESS you need to spend 20 hours, sometimes 2 hours, sometimes 200 hours, and sometimes 1,000 hours. (Old business generates itself, it needs an order of magnitude less time, because under that cash flow everything is already delegated, automated, optimized; the entrepreneur fights precisely for new business if things are more or less fine and the business isn't collapsing.)

What I build with my own hands without having to spend time and money on people, while also pumping up extremely valuable skills — that alone is …, and I'm not building just anything, I'm building precisely what makes every further invested hour increase profit in one form or another. Put 100 hours into something that then saves even 10 out of every following 100 hours — that's pure ROI pouring into your pocket after just 1,000 hours. 1,000 working hours is only one quarter, so in 4 months my lousy 100 hours start paying me back, for years. And these are all just example numbers. Reality is far tastier ;)

For some reason it didn't occur to me right away that Codex could be used like this:
1) Hey Codex, whip up a new project in the parent folder please, call it slsbmb-legal-finance

2) Hey Codex, go through all the PDF files in the downloads folder, find all the invoices that organizations X, Y, Z, K sent to their clients (any companies), and copy them into the root of the slsbmb-legal-finance project, split by year please.
(… a script that did this task across 2,800 invoices on the first try without a hitch!!!!)
3) Hey Codex, name all the invoices so they're mega easy to navigate: sequence number by date in ascending order (one digit, 1, 2, 3, etc.) — client name — month

4) Here are read-only keys for the banks; please cross-match which invoices ended up receiving money and which didn't. Be attentive to detail and don't mix things up. Look at references, dates, amounts if you need to; if some files are unclear, try to make an assumption; if you're not sure about the assumption, flag those files somehow and note it in the report — I'll double-check myself.

That way, in 20 minutes I got a folder with all the invoices of all the companies I run, with confidence that these are only the genuinely useful invoices (people who issue invoices know that the process produces a lot of junk, re-issued invoices with different properties, etc., and sorting that out by hand in a folder of 2,600 files is …, easier to shoot yourself).

And now I can just cd "project" and drop requests like “… the next invoice for Airvoice, check the numbers on all the invoices so the next one is definitely numbered right. The properties don't change (or if they do — you can just freestyle a note about what changed).
Or….

Here's a contract, please make an invoice from it for the HK company with the same properties as the other invoices, take all the details from the neighboring invoice, the last one issued for the HK company.
Or….
Please check, are all the invoices paid? The bank tokens are in a text file in the project folder.
The simplicity of this interaction is beyond comprehension, relative to its usefulness.
People sit and vibe-code themselves invoice management systems, with interfaces of some kind, but … are they needed for?
That's it, we're in the new Internet, where interfaces aren't needed, you just have to actually think your way to the simplest solution, and it sort of does itself =)))))
Well, I just did all of this, and it didn't make a mistake =)
I'm especially … that in 9 minutes it whipped up the scripts that helped it deal with 2,600 files and find exactly the ones it needed
By the way, I doubt the previous generation would have handled this task; I think only the very newest, just-released ones have learned to do this
